aws-route53-resolve.title: Route 53 Routing Policy Resolution
aws-route53-resolve.description:
Route 53 can answer the same DNS name differently depending on a **routing policy** and on the health
of the endpoints. Implement the choice.

`resolve(policy, records, query)` returns the **list of values** in the answer (`[]` = no answer).

Every record is a dict with `"value"` and `"healthy"` plus policy-specific fields. `query` is a dict
with what Route 53 knows about the request.

- **`"simple"`** — return all values in listed order; health is not considered.
- **`"multivalue"`** — return the values of the healthy records, at most the first 8; if no record is
  healthy, return the first 8 of all records.
- **`"weighted"`** — records have `"weight"` (integer ≥ 0). Candidates are the healthy records with
  weight > 0; if there are none, the candidates are all records with weight > 0 regardless of health
  (when everything looks down, Route 53 answers anyway). If **every** record has weight 0, treat every
  weight as 1 first. Let `total` be the sum of candidate weights and `r = query["roll"] % total`; walk
  the candidates in listed order subtracting weights and return the record in whose slice `r` falls
  (the first candidate owns `0 … w1-1`, the second `w1 … w1+w2-1`, and so on).
- **`"latency"`** — records have `"region"`; `query["latency"]` maps region → milliseconds measured
  from the user. Consider only records whose region appears in the map. Among the healthy ones return
  the record with the lowest latency (ties → first listed). If none is healthy, choose among all of
  them the same way.
- **`"failover"`** — records have `"role"`: exactly one `"PRIMARY"` and one `"SECONDARY"`. Return the
  primary if healthy; otherwise the secondary if healthy; otherwise the primary.
- **`"geolocation"`** — records have `"location"`: a country code, a continent code, or `"*"`
  (default). `query` has `"country"` and `"continent"`. Try, in order, the records whose location
  equals the country, then the continent, then `"*"`. At each level return the values of the
  **healthy** records of that level if there are any; otherwise fall through to the next level.
  Nothing left → `[]`.

**Example:** `resolve("failover", [primary unhealthy, secondary healthy], {})` → `["standby"]`

guide.prereqs: The Route 53 lesson: routing policies and health checks.
guide.intuition: Every policy is 'filter by health, then pick by a rule', with one shared safety net: if the health filter removes everything, Route 53 would rather return something than nothing.
hints: Write one branch per policy and test each alone.
Weighted: build the candidate list with its weights first, then a single cumulative walk using `roll % total`.
Geolocation is a three-level fallback loop over `(country, continent, '*')`.
guide.brute_force: For the weighted policy you could expand each record `weight` times into a list and index it with the roll: O(total weight) memory instead of O(records).
guide.approach: Dry run weighted with weights 70/20/10 where the first record is unhealthy and roll = 25: candidates are the 20 and the 10 → total 30 → r = 25 → not < 20, subtract → 5 < 10 → third record `3.3.3.3`. The unhealthy record's share is redistributed proportionally.
guide.complexity: O(R) time for R records, O(R) space.
guide.pitfalls: Returning nothing when all endpoints are unhealthy (weighted, latency, failover and multivalue all still answer); using the original total weight after filtering; ignoring ties in latency; letting an unhealthy country record block the fallback to continent.

aws-cloudfront-cache.title: CloudFront Cache Key and TTL
aws-cloudfront-cache.description:
A content delivery network stores responses under a **cache key** and keeps them for a **TTL** (time
to live, in seconds). Two requests share a cached copy only if their keys are identical, so the key
should contain exactly the parts of the request that change the response.

`cacheDecision(request, policy, cache_control)` returns `[cache_key, ttl]`.

- `request = {"path": "/img/a.png", "query": {name: value}, "headers": {name: value}}`.
- `policy = {"query": "none" | "all" | [names], "headers": [names], "min_ttl", "default_ttl", "max_ttl"}`.
- `cache_control`: the origin's `Cache-Control` response header (string) or `null` if absent.

**Cache key** = the path, then:

- the included query parameters (none, all, or only the listed names — query names are
  case-sensitive), sorted by name, written `name=value` and joined with `&`, preceded by `?` — omit
  the `?` when no parameter is included;
- then, for each header named in the policy that is present in the request (header names are
  **case-insensitive**), `|name=value` with the name lower-cased, sorted by lower-cased name.

**TTL.** Split `cache_control` on commas, trim spaces and lower-case the directives.

1. If it contains `no-store`, `no-cache` or `private` → `min_ttl`.
2. Else if it has `s-maxage=N` → `N` clamped to `[min_ttl, max_ttl]`.
3. Else if it has `max-age=N` → `N` clamped to `[min_ttl, max_ttl]`.
4. Else (no header, or none of these directives) → `default_ttl`.

**Example:** path `/img/a.png`, query `{"w":"200","utm_source":"mail"}`, header
`accept-language: fr`, policy query `["w","h"]`, headers `["Accept-Language"]`, min 60, default 86400,
max 31536000, `Cache-Control: max-age=10` → `["/img/a.png?w=200|accept-language=fr", 60]`

guide.prereqs: The CloudFront lesson: cache keys, cache policies and how the origin's Cache-Control interacts with minimum, default and maximum TTL.
guide.intuition: Two independent halves. The key is a canonical string: only whitelisted parts, in sorted order, so that equivalent requests collide on purpose. The TTL is a priority list over the origin's directives, squeezed between the policy's minimum and maximum.
hints: Build the key in three steps: path, sorted query part, sorted header part.
Lower-case request header names into a dict before looking anything up.
Parse directives into a clean list first; check the three 'do not cache' words, then `s-maxage`, then `max-age`.
guide.brute_force: Using the full URL and all headers as the key always gives correct content but a hit ratio near zero — tracking parameters such as `utm_source` would split every object into thousands of copies.
guide.approach: Dry run of the example: included query names = {w} (utm_source is not whitelisted) → `?w=200`; policy header Accept-Language is present (case-insensitively) → `|accept-language=fr`. Directives `[max-age=10]` → 10 clamped to at least 60 → 60.
guide.complexity: O(q log q + h log h) for q query parameters and h headers; O(key length) space.
guide.pitfalls: Leaving a dangling `?`; case-sensitive header matching; letting `max-age` win over `s-maxage`; returning 0 for `no-cache` instead of the minimum TTL; forgetting to clamp.

aws-sns-filter-fanout.title: SNS Fan-Out with Filter Policies
aws-sns-filter-fanout.description:
An SNS **topic** copies each published message to all its subscriptions (fan-out). A subscription may
carry a **filter policy** so that it receives only the messages whose attributes match.

`deliver(subscriptions, attributes)` returns the names of the subscriptions that receive the message,
in the given order.

- `subscriptions`: list of `[name, policy]`; `policy` is `null` or `{}` (receive everything) or a dict
  `attribute_name -> list of rules`.
- `attributes`: the message attributes, a dict `name -> string or number`.
- A policy matches when **every** attribute name in it is satisfied (AND), and a name is satisfied
  when **at least one** rule in its list matches (OR). Rules:
  - a plain string or number: the attribute exists and equals it exactly (`"5"` and `5` are different);
  - `{"prefix": "abc"}`: the attribute exists, is a string and starts with `abc`;
  - `{"anything-but": [v1, v2, ...]}`: the attribute exists and is not equal to any listed value;
  - `{"numeric": [op, n]}` with `op` in `">"`, `">="`, `"<"`, `"<="`, `"="`: the attribute exists, is
    a number (not a string, not a boolean) and satisfies the comparison;
  - `{"exists": true}`: the attribute exists; `{"exists": false}`: the attribute does **not** exist.
- If the attribute is absent, only `{"exists": false}` can match.

**Example:** policy `{"type": ["order"], "amount": [{"numeric": [">=", 1000]}]}` with attributes
`{"type": "order", "amount": 1500}` matches; with `amount: 200` it does not.

guide.prereqs: The SQS and SNS lesson: topics, subscriptions, fan-out and filter policies.
guide.intuition: AND across attribute names, OR across the rules of one name. Write a function that judges one rule against one attribute and the rest is two nested loops.
hints: Pass three things to the rule checker: the rule, whether the attribute is present, and its value.
Handle `exists` first — it is the only rule that can match an absent attribute.
Strings and numbers never equal each other here; check the types before comparing.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable; matching is linear in the size of the policy.
guide.approach: Dry run of the fourth test (refund, eu-west-1, amount 5000, env test, no key, no user): audit → no policy → yes. eu-orders → region ok, type refund ≠ order → no. big-orders → type fails → no. not-test → env is `test`, which is excluded → no. images → `key` absent → prefix cannot match → no. anonymous → `user` absent and rule is exists:false → yes. Result `[audit, anonymous]`.
guide.complexity: O(S × P) for S subscriptions and P rules per policy.
guide.pitfalls: Using OR between attribute names; matching `anything-but` when the attribute is absent; treating the string '1500' as the number 1500; `True` passing as a number in Python (`isinstance(True, int)` is true).

aws-sqs-simulator.title: SQS Queue Simulator
aws-sqs-simulator.description:
Build a small in-memory model of an SQS queue. Every method receives the current time `t` explicitly
(integer seconds, never decreasing across calls) — there is no real clock.

```
Queue(visibility_timeout, max_receive, fifo)
send(t, body, group)        -> message id (1, 2, 3, ... in send order)
receive(t, max_n)           -> list of [id, body, receipt]
delete(t, receipt)          -> True / False
dlq(t)                      -> list of message ids moved to the dead-letter queue, in order
```

**Visibility timeout.** A received message is not removed. It becomes invisible until
`t + visibility_timeout`; if it is not deleted by then, it becomes visible again and can be received
again (this is how SQS gives *at-least-once* delivery).

**receive(t, max_n).** Scan the stored messages in send order and collect up to `max_n` messages that
are visible at `t` (`visible_at <= t`). For each visible message in the scan:

- if it has already been received `max_receive` times, move it to the dead-letter queue instead (it
  leaves this queue, is not returned and does not count towards `max_n`);
- otherwise increment its receive count, hide it until `t + visibility_timeout` and return
  `[id, body, receipt]` where `receipt` is the string `"<id>:<receive_count>"`.

**FIFO mode** (`fifo=True`). Messages have a `group` (a string). Within a group, order is strict:
only the **oldest remaining** message of each group can be considered, and while it is invisible
(in flight) the whole group is blocked. One `receive` call returns at most one message per group.
If the oldest message of a group is moved to the dead-letter queue during a scan, the next message of
that group is considered in the same scan. In standard mode (`fifo=False`), `group` is ignored.

**delete(t, receipt).** Succeeds (returns `True` and removes the message) only if the message is
still in this queue and the receipt is the one from its **most recent** receive. A stale receipt, an
unknown one, or a message already deleted or dead-lettered → `False`.

Tests use the LeetCode design format: a list of method names and a list of argument lists.

guide.prereqs: The SQS and SNS lesson: visibility timeout, at-least-once delivery, dead-letter queues, FIFO message groups.
guide.intuition: A message is a small record: when it becomes visible again and how many times it has been handed out. `receive` is a single ordered scan that either skips, dead-letters or hands out each message. FIFO adds one set: the groups already blocked or served in this scan.
hints: Store `visible_at` (initially the send time) and `count` per message; a message is in flight exactly when `visible_at > t`.
Check the dead-letter condition **before** incrementing the count: a message received `max_receive` times moves on its next visible scan.
In FIFO mode add the group to a `blocked` set both when you return its head and when its head is invisible — but not when the head is dead-lettered.
guide.brute_force: Advancing a simulated clock second by second and expiring timers is unnecessary: comparing `visible_at` with the `t` passed in gives the same behaviour lazily.
guide.approach: Dry run of the second test (timeout 10, max_receive 2): send at 0. receive(0) → count 1, receipt `1:1`, hidden until 10. receive(10) → visible again → count 2, receipt `1:2`, hidden until 20. receive(20) → count is already 2 = max → moved to the dead-letter queue, returns `[]`. receive(30) → `[]`. dlq → `[1]`. delete(`1:2`) → False, the message is no longer in this queue.
guide.complexity: `receive` and `delete` are O(n) in the number of stored messages; `send` is O(1). Space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Removing a message on receive; accepting stale receipts; counting dead-lettered messages towards `max_n`; in FIFO mode delivering the second message of a group while the first is in flight; accepting the receipt `id:0` for a message never received.
guide.follow_up: Real FIFO queues also deduplicate sends for five minutes using a deduplication id, and can return several messages of one group in a single batch, in order.

aws-kinesis-shards.title: Kinesis Shard Count and Partition Keys
aws-kinesis-shards.description:
A Kinesis data stream in provisioned mode is made of **shards**. Each shard accepts at most
**1,024 KB/s and 1,000 records/s** of writes and serves at most **2,048 KB/s** of reads. Each record
has a **partition key**; the MD5 hash of the key (a 128-bit number) decides the shard, and the shards
split the hash range `0 … 2^128 - 1` into equal consecutive slices.

`shardPlan(write_kb_per_s, records_per_s, read_kb_per_s, keys)`:

1. Compute the number of shards needed:
   `n = max(1, ceil(write_kb_per_s / 1024), ceil(records_per_s / 1000), ceil(read_kb_per_s / 2048))`.
2. For each partition key in `keys` (a list of strings, one per record of a sample; keys repeat),
   compute `h = int(md5(key as UTF-8).hexdigest(), 16)` and the shard index `h * n // 2**128`.
3. Return `[n, counts]` where `counts[i]` is the number of sample records landing on shard `i`.

Use `hashlib.md5`. All inputs are non-negative integers.

**Example:** `shardPlan(3000, 500, 1000, ["user-1", "user-2", "user-1"])` → 3 shards (write volume is
the constraint) and the two `user-1` records necessarily share a shard.
aws-kinesis-shards.solution:
import hashlib

def shardPlan(write_kb_per_s, records_per_s, read_kb_per_s, keys):
    n = max(1, -(-write_kb_per_s // 1024), -(-records_per_s // 1000), -(-read_kb_per_s // 2048))
    counts = [0] * n
    for k in keys:
        h = int(hashlib.md5(k.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest(), 16)
        counts[h * n // 2 ** 128] += 1
    return [n, counts]

guide.prereqs: The Kinesis lesson: shards, per-shard limits and partition keys. `hashlib` and integer ceiling division.
guide.intuition: Capacity planning is 'the tightest of three limits'. Routing is range partitioning of a hash: scale the 128-bit hash down to an index with multiply-then-divide.
hints: Ceiling division: `-(-a // b)`.
`int(hexdigest, 16)` gives the 128-bit integer.
`h * n // 2**128` maps the range evenly to `0 … n-1`; this is not the same as `h % n`.
guide.brute_force: Building explicit `(start, end)` hash ranges per shard and scanning them for every key is O(keys × shards); the arithmetic mapping is O(keys).
guide.approach: Dry run for the example: ceil(3000/1024) = 3, ceil(500/1000) = 1, ceil(1000/2048) = 1 → 3 shards. Hash each key and compute the slice. Identical keys always produce the same hash, so thirty records with the key `tenant-42` land on one shard no matter how many shards exist — a hot shard that adding shards cannot fix.
guide.complexity: O(k × L) for k keys of length L; O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Floor instead of ceiling; modulo instead of range partitioning (real streams use ranges, which is why a shard can be split in two); forgetting the minimum of one shard; forgetting to encode the key as UTF-8.

aws-subnet-public-private.title: Public, Private or Isolated Subnet?
aws-subnet-public-private.description:
Nothing in a subnet's own settings says "public". A subnet is public **only because of its route
table**: its default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) points at an internet gateway.

Write `classifySubnets(subnets, route_tables, main_table)`:

- `subnets`: dict `subnet_id -> route_table_id`, or `null` when the subnet has no explicit association
  and therefore uses the VPC's **main route table** `main_table`.
- `route_tables`: dict `route_table_id -> list of [destination_cidr, target]`.
- Look only at the route whose destination is exactly `"0.0.0.0/0"`:
  - target starts with `"igw-"` → `"public"`
  - target starts with `"nat-"` → `"private"`
  - no such route → `"isolated"`
  - any other target (`tgw-`, `vgw-`, `eni-`, …) → `"private-custom"`

Return a dict `subnet_id -> classification`.

**Example:** `{"subnet-a": "rtb-1", "subnet-b": null}` with `rtb-1 = [["10.0.0.0/16","local"],["0.0.0.0/0","igw-1"]]`,
main `rtb-0 = [["10.0.0.0/16","local"]]` → `{"subnet-a": "public", "subnet-b": "isolated"}`

guide.prereqs: The VPC basics lesson: route tables, the main route table, internet and NAT gateways.
guide.intuition: Follow the pointer: subnet → its route table (or the main one) → the default route → the kind of target.
hints: Resolve `None` to `main_table` before anything else.
Only the destination `0.0.0.0/0` matters; an `igw-` target on a narrower route does not make the subnet public.
Use `startswith` on the target id.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable — the direct lookup is linear in the number of routes.
guide.approach: Dry run: subnet `s1` uses `rtb-partial` = `[10.0.0.0/16 → local, 8.8.8.0/24 → igw]`. There is no `0.0.0.0/0` entry, so the subnet is `isolated` for our purposes even though one narrow range goes to the internet gateway.
guide.complexity: O(total routes examined) time, O(subnets) space.
guide.pitfalls: Declaring a subnet public because an `igw-` target appears anywhere in the table; forgetting the main route table fallback; assuming the main table is private.

aws-route-longest-prefix.title: Route Table Longest-Prefix Match
aws-route-longest-prefix.description:
When a packet leaves a subnet, the VPC router picks the route whose destination range contains the
packet's destination address **and is the most specific** (the longest prefix, i.e. the largest number
after the slash). The order of the routes in the table does not matter.

Write `routeTarget(routes, ip)`:

- `routes`: list of `[cidr, target]`, with distinct CIDR blocks such as `"10.0.0.0/16"` or `"0.0.0.0/0"`.
- `ip`: a dotted IPv4 address.
- Return the target of the most specific matching route, or `"no-route"` if none matches.

A CIDR block `a.b.c.d/n` contains an address when their first `n` bits are equal.

**Example:** routes `[["10.0.0.0/16","local"],["0.0.0.0/0","nat-1"],["10.20.0.0/16","pcx-9"]]`:
`10.0.3.7` → `"local"`, `10.20.1.1` → `"pcx-9"`, `52.1.2.3` → `"nat-1"`.

guide.prereqs: The VPC basics lesson (CIDR notation, route tables). Bit operations: shift and mask.
guide.intuition: Convert addresses to 32-bit integers. A route matches when the top `n` bits agree; among matches keep the largest `n`.
hints: `(a << 24) | (b << 16) | (c << 8) | d` turns four octets into one integer.
The mask for `/n` has `n` one-bits at the top: `(0xFFFFFFFF << (32 - n)) & 0xFFFFFFFF`; treat `/0` separately or note that it yields 0.
Track `best_len` starting at -1 so that a `/0` route can win when nothing else matches.
guide.brute_force: Scanning every route is already optimal for a list (real routers use a trie for millions of prefixes).
guide.approach: Dry run for `10.1.2.4` with routes `/0 igw`, `10.0.0.0/8 tgw`, `10.1.0.0/16 pcx`, `10.1.2.0/24 eni-1`, `10.1.2.3/32 eni-2`: the first four match, the `/32` does not (last bit pattern differs). The longest match is `/24` → `eni-1`.
guide.complexity: O(R) time for R routes, O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: Returning the first match instead of the most specific; comparing dotted strings with `startswith` (breaks for prefixes that are not multiples of 8 and for `192.168.1` vs `192.168.10`); a mask that overflows 32 bits in Python.

aws-vpc-subnet-planner.title: VPC Subnet Planner
aws-vpc-subnet-planner.description:
Carve a VPC's address range into non-overlapping subnets: one subnet per **tier** (public, app, data…)
in each **Availability Zone**.

Write `planSubnets(vpc_cidr, azs, tiers)`:

- `vpc_cidr`: for example `"10.0.0.0/16"` (always a valid, aligned block).
- `azs`: list of AZ names, e.g. `["a", "b", "c"]`.
- `tiers`: list of `[tier_name, prefix_length]`, e.g. `[["public", 24], ["app", 22]]`.
- Allocate in this order: tiers in the given order, and for each tier the AZs in the given order.
  Each request takes the **lowest-addressed** block of the requested size that is correctly aligned
  (its start address is a multiple of its size), lies inside the VPC and does not overlap any block
  allocated so far.
- AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet (network, router, DNS, future use, broadcast), so the
  usable host count is `2^(32 - prefix) - 5`.
- Return a list of `[tier_name, az, subnet_cidr, usable_hosts]` in allocation order.
- Return `[]` if any prefix is smaller than the VPC's prefix or larger than 28 (the AWS subnet size
  limits are /16 to /28), or if some request cannot be satisfied.

**Example:** `planSubnets("10.0.0.0/24", ["a","b"], [["web", 26]])`
→ `[["web","a","10.0.0.0/26",59], ["web","b","10.0.0.64/26",59]]`

guide.prereqs: The VPC basics lesson (CIDR arithmetic, the five reserved addresses). Integer representation of IPv4 addresses.
guide.intuition: A block of prefix `p` has size `2^(32-p)` and can only start at a multiple of that size. For each request, slide along the aligned positions until the block overlaps nothing taken — a first-fit allocator.
hints: Convert the VPC to `[base, end)` as integers; keep a list of taken `(start, end)` intervals.
Two half-open intervals overlap when `a_start < b_end and b_start < a_end`.
When a candidate clashes with a taken block, jump to the next aligned start at or after that block's end instead of stepping one block at a time.
guide.brute_force: A moving cursor that never looks back is the tempting approach; it wastes or mis-aligns space when a large block follows a small one and it can never reuse the gap left behind. Trying every aligned position one by one is correct but can test thousands of positions.
guide.approach: Dry run: VPC `10.0.0.0/24`, AZs a,b, tiers `small /28`, `mid /26`, `tiny /28`. small-a → .0/28, small-b → .16/28. mid (size 64): .0 clashes → jump past .16 block's end (32) aligned up to 64 → `.64/26`, then `.128/26`. tiny: .0 and .16 taken, `.32/28` is free and aligned → tiny-a, then `.48/28`. The gap left by alignment is reused.
guide.complexity: O(N²) in the number of subnets N in the worst case (each request scans the taken list a few times); O(N) space.
guide.pitfalls: Unaligned subnets (10.0.0.32/26 is not a valid block); subtracting 2 instead of 5; accepting /29 or a prefix shorter than the VPC's; returning a partial plan instead of `[]`.

aws-sg-nacl-evaluate.title: Security Group and Network ACL Evaluation
aws-sg-nacl-evaluate.description:
A client opens a connection to an EC2 instance. Two firewalls stand in the way:

- the subnet's **network ACL** — *stateless*, numbered rules, allow **and** deny;
- the instance's **security group** — *stateful*, allow rules only.

Write `packetVerdict(packet, sg_inbound, nacl_inbound, nacl_outbound)`.

`packet = {"src": client_ip, "protocol": "tcp"|"udp", "dst_port": int, "src_port": int}` describes the
request. The reply travels back to `src` on port `src_port` (the client's ephemeral port).

**Network ACL rule**: `[number, protocol, port_from, port_to, cidr, "allow"|"deny"]`. Protocol `"-1"`
means all protocols and its port range is ignored. Rules are evaluated in **ascending rule number**
(the list may be unsorted); the **first** rule that matches decides. If no rule matches, the packet is
denied (the implicit `*` rule).

**Security group rule**: `[protocol, port_from, port_to, cidr]` (protocol `"-1"` = everything). If
**any** rule matches the packet is allowed; otherwise it is denied.

A rule matches when the protocol matches, the relevant port is within `[port_from, port_to]`, and the
relevant address is inside `cidr`.

Evaluate in this order and return the first failure:

1. Inbound NACL against the request (`src` address, `dst_port`) → else `"NACL_INBOUND_DENY"`.
2. Security group inbound against the request → else `"SG_DENY"`.
3. The reply: the security group is stateful, so the reply is allowed automatically. The outbound
   NACL is stateless and must allow the reply (address `src`, port `src_port`) → else
   `"NACL_OUTBOUND_DENY"`.
4. Otherwise `"ALLOWED"`.

**Example:** inbound NACL allows tcp 443 from anywhere, SG allows tcp 443, outbound NACL allows only
tcp 443 → a request from port 50000 gets `"NACL_OUTBOUND_DENY"`: the reply to port 50000 is dropped.
aws-sg-nacl-evaluate.starter:
def packetVerdict(packet, sg_inbound, nacl_inbound, nacl_outbound):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The security groups versus network ACLs lesson; CIDR membership from the longest-prefix problem.
guide.intuition: Three checkpoints in sequence. The ACL is a sorted first-match list and is consulted twice — once per direction — because it has no memory. The security group is an any-match list and is consulted once because it remembers the connection.
hints: Write one `match(rule fields, protocol, port, ip)` helper and reuse it for both firewalls.
For the ACL, sort by rule number and return at the first matching rule, whether it says allow or deny.
For the reply, the port to test is the client's `src_port` and the address is still the client's address.
guide.brute_force: Treating the ACL like IAM ('any deny wins, otherwise any allow') ignores rule numbers and gives wrong answers when an allow rule has a lower number than a deny rule.
guide.approach: Dry run: request from 198.51.100.7:50000 to port 443; inbound ACL `[200 allow 443 from all, 100 deny all tcp from 198.51.100.0/24]`. Sorted: rule 100 matches first → deny → `NACL_INBOUND_DENY`. Swap the numbers and rule 100 (allow 443) matches first → continue to the security group.
guide.complexity: O(R log R) for sorting the ACL rules plus O(R) matching; O(R) space for the sorted copy.
guide.pitfalls: Skipping the outbound ACL check; checking the reply against `dst_port`; assuming the ACL list is already sorted; forgetting that protocol `-1` ignores ports; adding a security-group outbound check for the reply (stateful firewalls do not need one).

aws-ec2-purchase-cost.title: On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot
aws-ec2-purchase-cost.description:
Choose the cheapest way to pay for one instance during a 730-hour month. All money is in **integer
cents** so that no rounding is needed.

`cheapestPlan(job)` where `job` is a dict:

- `hours`: hours of work the instance must complete this month (0–730).
- `od_rate`: On-Demand price, cents per hour. Cost = `hours × od_rate`.
- `ri_monthly`: fixed monthly fee of a reservation, in cents (the amortised upfront part), and
  `ri_rate`: its hourly rate. A reservation is billed for **all 730 hours** whether the instance runs
  or not: cost = `ri_monthly + 730 × ri_rate`.
- `spot_rate`: Spot price, cents per hour. `interruptions`: how many times the instance is reclaimed
  during the month. Each interruption wastes `rework_hours` of progress that must be run again:
  cost = `(hours + interruptions × rework_hours) × spot_rate`.
- `interruptible`: if `False` the workload cannot tolerate interruption and Spot is not an option.
- Spot is also not an option if the total Spot hours `hours + interruptions × rework_hours` exceed 730.

Return `[plan, cost_in_cents]` with `plan` in `"on-demand"`, `"reserved"`, `"spot"`. On a tie prefer
on-demand, then reserved, then spot (the least commitment and the least risk first).

**Example:** 200 hours, On-Demand 10 c/h, reservation 0 + 6 c/h, Spot 3 c/h with 4 interruptions of 5
hours, interruptible → on-demand 2000, reserved 4380, spot 660 → `["spot", 660]`.

guide.prereqs: The EC2 purchasing lesson: how each option is billed and what an interruption costs.
guide.intuition: Write the three cost formulas exactly as the billing rules state them, drop the options that are not allowed, and take the minimum with a stable tie-break.
hints: A reservation's cost does not depend on `hours` at all.
Compute the Spot hours first; they decide both eligibility and cost.
Build the option list in tie-break order and replace the best only on a strictly smaller cost.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable; the pitfall is modelling, not speed.
guide.approach: Dry run: 438 hours, OD 10, RI 0 + 6/h, Spot 9 with 30 interruptions × 2 h. On-demand 4380; reserved 730 × 6 = 4380; spot (438 + 60) × 9 = 4482. Tie between on-demand and reserved → on-demand. At 439 hours on-demand becomes 4390 and reserved wins: the break-even utilisation is `ri_rate / od_rate` = 60 % of the month.
guide.pitfalls: Charging the reservation only for the hours used; ignoring rework after interruptions; offering Spot to a workload that cannot be interrupted; an unstable tie-break from `min` over a differently ordered list.

aws-right-size.title: Right-Size an Instance
aws-right-size.description:
Right-sizing means replacing an instance with the cheapest type that still fits the measured load plus
a safety margin.

`rightSize(current, catalog, cpu_p95, mem_p95, headroom)`:

- `catalog`: list of `[name, vcpus, memory_gib, price_cents_per_hour]` (all integers). `current` is the
  name of one of them.
- `cpu_p95`, `mem_p95`: the 95th-percentile utilisation over the last two weeks, as integer
  percentages **of the current instance's** vCPUs and memory.
- `headroom`: integer percentage of extra capacity to keep free.
- Required capacity: `needed_vcpu = current_vcpus × cpu_p95/100 × (1 + headroom/100)` and likewise for
  memory. A candidate fits when its vCPUs **and** memory are both at least the needed amounts
  (fractions matter: 2.1 needed vCPUs do not fit on 2).
- Return the name of the cheapest fitting instance; break price ties by the alphabetically smallest
  name. If nothing fits (the instance is overloaded and no bigger type exists), return `current`.

Use integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point surprises:
`candidate_vcpus × 10000 >= current_vcpus × cpu_p95 × (100 + headroom)`.

**Example:** current `m6i.xlarge` (4 vCPU, 16 GiB), CPU p95 20 %, memory p95 40 %, headroom 20 % →
needs 0.96 vCPU and 7.68 GiB → the cheapest type with at least 8 GiB.
aws-right-size.starter:
def rightSize(current, catalog, cpu_p95, mem_p95, headroom):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The EC2 purchasing and right-sizing lesson; tuples compare element by element in Python.
guide.intuition: Translate percentages of the current machine into absolute needs, inflate by the headroom, then run a filtered minimum over the catalogue.
hints: Find the current row first — every percentage is relative to it.
Multiply everything out to avoid division: compare `vcpu × 10000` with `cur_vcpu × p95 × (100 + headroom)`.
Use the tuple `(price, name)` as the sort key so that the tie-break comes for free.
guide.brute_force: Sorting the whole catalogue by price and scanning is O(n log n); a single pass with a running best is O(n).
guide.approach: Dry run: current m6i.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB), CPU 10 %, memory 45 %, headroom 10 %. Needs 0.88 vCPU and 15.84 GiB. Types with ≥ 16 GiB: r6i.large (1260), m6i.xlarge (1920), m6i.2xlarge (3840) → `r6i.large`. At 46 % memory the need is 16.19 GiB, so only m6i.2xlarge fits → stay.
guide.complexity: O(n) time over the catalogue, O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: Integer division that floors the requirement; forgetting headroom; only considering cheaper types (an overloaded instance should be allowed to grow — but here, when nothing fits we keep the current one); ignoring the name tie-break.

aws-ebs-performance.title: EBS Volume IOPS and Throughput
aws-ebs-performance.description:
Each EBS volume type has its own rules linking size, **IOPS** (input/output operations per second) and
**throughput** (MiB per second). Implement the rules below (a simplified version of the published
limits) and reject impossible configurations.

`ebsPerformance(volume_type, size_gib, iops, throughput)` returns `[iops, throughput_mib_s]`, or `[]`
when the configuration is invalid. `iops` and `throughput` are the provisioned values or `null` for
"use the default".

| type | size (GiB) | IOPS | throughput (MiB/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gp2` | 1–16384 | `min(16000, max(100, 3 × size))`; provisioned values are ignored | 128 if size ≤ 170, otherwise 250 |
| `gp3` | 1–65536 | default 3000; valid 3000–80000 and at most `500 × size` | default 125; valid 125–2000 and at most `0.25 × IOPS` |
| `io2` | 4–65536 | **required**; valid 100–256000 and at most `1000 × size` | `min(4000, IOPS × 256 // 1024)`; provisioned value ignored |
| `st1` | 125–16384 | always 500 (provisioned value ignored) | `min(500, 40 × size // 1024)` |

For `gp3`, the default IOPS of 3000 is always valid, whatever the size. Any other volume type, or a
size outside the range, or an invalid provisioned value → `[]`.

**Example:** `ebsPerformance("gp3", 100, 12000, 500)` → `[12000, 500]`;
`ebsPerformance("gp3", 10, 6000, null)` → `[]` (10 GiB allows at most 5000 IOPS).
aws-ebs-performance.starter:
def ebsPerformance(volume_type, size_gib, iops, throughput):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The EBS lesson: what IOPS and throughput mean and how gp2, gp3, io2 and st1 differ.
guide.intuition: One branch per volume type. In each branch validate the size, then the provisioned numbers, then compute what the volume delivers. gp2 and st1 derive performance from size; gp3 and io2 let you buy it, within ratios.
hints: Handle `None` defaults before range checks.
The gp3 throughput rule `≤ 0.25 × IOPS` is safest as `throughput × 4 <= iops`.
A 1 GiB gp3 volume still gets 3000 IOPS — the `500 × size` ratio only limits IOPS provisioned above the baseline.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable — this is rule transcription; the risk is missing a boundary.
guide.approach: Dry run `gp3, 100 GiB, iops 3000, throughput 751`: size fine; IOPS at baseline; throughput in range but 751 × 4 = 3004 > 3000 → invalid → `[]`. With 750 the product equals 3000 → `[3000, 750]`.
guide.pitfalls: Rejecting small gp3 volumes at the default 3000 IOPS; forgetting the gp2 floor of 100 IOPS and cap of 16000; letting io2 run without provisioned IOPS; not rejecting unknown types.

aws-az-failure-capacity.title: Capacity That Survives an AZ Failure
aws-az-failure-capacity.description:
An Auto Scaling group spreads identical instances evenly over `zones` Availability Zones (the same
number in each). You want **static stability**: if any one zone disappears, the instances that are
left must carry the peak load straight away, without waiting for new ones.

`azCapacity(peak_rps, rps_per_instance, zones, max_util_pct)`:

- `peak_rps`: requests per second at peak (integer, 0 or more).
- `rps_per_instance`: requests per second one instance handles when fully busy (integer, 1 or more).
- `zones`: number of Availability Zones in use (2 or more).
- `max_util_pct`: instances should run at no more than this percentage of full capacity
  (integer 1 to 100), so one instance may be given at most `rps_per_instance * max_util_pct / 100`
  requests per second.

Return `[per_zone, total]`: the smallest number of instances per zone, and the fleet total, such that
the instances in any `zones - 1` zones can serve `peak_rps` within the utilisation limit. There is
always at least one instance per zone.

**Example:** `azCapacity(900, 150, 2, 100)` → `[6, 12]` (six instances serve the peak, and each zone
must hold all six).

**Example:** `azCapacity(900, 150, 3, 100)` → `[3, 9]` (two surviving zones hold six between them).
aws-az-failure-capacity.starter:
def azCapacity(peak_rps, rps_per_instance, zones, max_util_pct):
    pass
aws-az-failure-capacity.solution:
def azCapacity(peak_rps, rps_per_instance, zones, max_util_pct):
    usable = rps_per_instance * max_util_pct            # capacity of one instance, in hundredths
    needed = -(-peak_rps * 100 // usable)                # ceiling division, integers only
    per_zone = max(1, -(-needed // (zones - 1)))
    return [per_zone, per_zone * zones]

guide.prereqs: Project part 2 (static stability) and the Auto Scaling lesson. Ceiling division.
guide.intuition: Work out how many instances the peak needs at the allowed utilisation. Those instances must all fit in the zones that remain after one is lost, so divide by `zones - 1`, not by `zones`.
hints: How many instances serve the peak if each may only be loaded to `max_util_pct`?
After a zone fails, `zones - 1` zones are left. They must hold that many instances between them.
Round up twice: once for instances needed, once for instances per zone. `-(-a // b)` is ceiling division with integers.
guide.brute_force: Try per_zone = 1, 2, 3, ... and stop at the first value where `per_zone * (zones - 1) * usable capacity >= peak`. Correct but linear in the answer.
guide.approach: Dry run `azCapacity(900, 150, 3, 60)`: one instance may take 150 x 0.60 = 90 requests/s, so the peak needs ceil(900 / 90) = 10 instances. Two zones survive, so each zone needs ceil(10 / 2) = 5, and the fleet is 15. Check: lose a zone, 10 instances x 90 = 900. Keep the arithmetic in integers (multiply the peak by 100 instead of dividing the capacity) to avoid floating-point surprises.
guide.complexity: O(1) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Dividing by `zones` (sizes for normal running only); forgetting the utilisation limit; rounding down; returning 0 per zone when the peak is 0; using floats, where 0.7 x 100 is not exactly 70.
guide.follow_up: With two zones the fleet is 100 % over-provisioned, with three zones 50 %, with four 33 %. That is the cost argument for using three zones.

aws-rolling-deploy-plan.title: Instance Refresh Plan
aws-rolling-deploy-plan.description:
An Auto Scaling group of `fleet` instances must be replaced with a new version by an **instance
refresh**. Two settings bound what may happen while it runs:

- `min_healthy_pct` (0 to 100): at least `ceil(fleet * min_healthy_pct / 100)` instances must be
  healthy and in service at every moment.
- `max_healthy_pct` (100 to 200): the group may temporarily grow to at most
  `floor(fleet * max_healthy_pct / 100)` instances.

So in one round the group may launch up to `surge = ceiling - fleet` extra new instances first, and
take up to `dip = fleet - floor_healthy` old instances out of service straight away.

Each round replaces `batch = min(old instances remaining, surge + dip)` instances like this:

1. Launch `min(batch, surge)` new instances; the total rises by that amount.
2. At the same time terminate the other `batch - min(batch, surge)` old instances; the healthy count
   dips by that amount until their replacements are ready.
3. When all new instances are healthy, terminate the old ones that step 1 kept; the group is back at
   `fleet`.

Return a list with one entry per round: `[batch, lowest_healthy, highest_total]`, where
`lowest_healthy` is the smallest number of healthy instances during the round and `highest_total`
the largest group size. If no instance can ever be replaced (`surge + dip == 0`), return `[]`.

**Example:** `rollingDeploy(4, 50, 100)` → `[[2, 2, 4], [2, 2, 4]]`

**Example:** `rollingDeploy(4, 100, 150)` → `[[2, 4, 6], [2, 4, 6]]` (launch before terminate: capacity never dips)
aws-rolling-deploy-plan.solution:
def rollingDeploy(fleet, min_healthy_pct, max_healthy_pct):
    floor_healthy = -(-fleet * min_healthy_pct // 100)     # ceiling
    ceiling = fleet * max_healthy_pct // 100               # floor
    surge = ceiling - fleet
    dip = fleet - floor_healthy
    if surge + dip == 0:
        return []
    rounds, remaining = [], fleet
    while remaining > 0:
        batch = min(remaining, surge + dip)
        launched_first = min(batch, surge)
        rounds.append([batch, fleet - (batch - launched_first), fleet + launched_first])
        remaining -= batch
    return rounds

guide.prereqs: Project part 2 (shipping changes safely) and the Auto Scaling lesson on instance refresh.
guide.intuition: Two budgets exist per round: how far the group may grow (surge) and how far healthy capacity may fall (dip). A round replaces as many instances as the two budgets together allow, spending the surge budget first because it costs no capacity.
hints: Compute the healthy floor with a ceiling and the size limit with a floor; both must be integers.
`surge = ceiling - fleet`, `dip = fleet - floor_healthy`, and a round handles at most `surge + dip` instances.
In the last round the batch may be smaller than the budgets. Launch-first covers `min(batch, surge)` of it; only the rest causes a dip.
guide.brute_force: Simulate instance by instance with explicit lists of old and new servers and their states. It gives the same numbers with far more code.
guide.approach: Dry run `rollingDeploy(9, 67, 133)`: floor_healthy = ceil(6.03) = 7, ceiling = floor(11.97) = 11, so surge = 2 and dip = 2. Round 1: batch 4, launch 2 first (total 11), terminate 2 at once (healthy 7). Round 2: the same. Round 3: one instance left, launched first, so healthy stays 9 and total peaks at 10. Result `[[4,7,11],[4,7,11],[1,9,10]]`.
guide.complexity: O(fleet / batch) rounds, O(1) work per round.
guide.pitfalls: Rounding the healthy floor down (it would allow dipping below the minimum); ignoring the surge budget; reporting the full dip and surge in a final, smaller round; looping for ever when both budgets are zero.
guide.follow_up: Setting the minimum to 100 % and the maximum above 100 % gives a deployment with no loss of capacity, at the price of briefly paying for extra instances.

aws-composite-availability.title: Availability of a Design
aws-composite-availability.description:
In a design review you are asked how available the whole system is, given the availability of its parts.

A design is described recursively:

- a number such as `99.9` is one component that is available that percentage of the time;
- `["serial", [parts...]]` is a chain in which **every** part must work (a load balancer, then a
  server, then a database);
- `["parallel", [parts...]]` is a redundant group that works if **at least one** part works
  (two servers behind a load balancer). Failures are assumed independent.

`compositeAvailability(design)` returns `[availability_pct, downtime_minutes_per_year]` for the whole
design, where a year has 365 days (525,600 minutes). An empty serial group is 100 % available.

**Example:** `["serial", [99.9, 99.9]]` → `[99.8001, 1050.6744]`

**Example:** `["parallel", [99.0, 99.0]]` → `[99.99, 52.56]`

Answers are compared with a small tolerance.

guide.prereqs: The reliability lesson (availability in numbers) and the design-answers lesson. Recursion over nested lists.
guide.intuition: A chain works only if every link works, so multiply availabilities. A redundant group fails only if every member fails, so multiply the failure probabilities and subtract from one.
hints: Convert percentages to fractions first: 99.9 becomes 0.999.
Serial: product of the parts. Parallel: one minus the product of (1 - part).
A part may itself be a serial or parallel group, so write a helper that calls itself.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate every combination of up/down for all leaf components and add the probabilities of the combinations in which the system works: O(2^n). The recursive formula is O(n).
guide.approach: Dry run `['serial', [99.99, ['parallel', [99.5, 99.5]], 99.95]]`: the parallel pair fails with probability 0.005 x 0.005 = 0.000025, so it is 0.999975 available. The chain is 0.9999 x 0.999975 x 0.9995 = 0.999375..., about 99.9375 %, or roughly 328 minutes of downtime a year. Notice that the redundant pair is now better than either single component beside it.
guide.complexity: O(n) time for n leaf components; recursion depth equals the nesting depth.
guide.pitfalls: Multiplying availabilities for a parallel group (that describes a chain); taking min or max instead of combining probabilities; forgetting to convert between percent and fraction; treating an empty chain as 0 %.
guide.follow_up: Real failures are not independent: two servers in the same Availability Zone share its fate. That is why redundancy must span zones, and why the result of this formula is an upper bound.

aws-spot-training-steps.title: Spot Training With Checkpoints
aws-spot-training-steps.description:
A training job runs on Spot capacity, which can be taken away. Time is counted in equal **steps**
(say, quarter hours), and every step the job runs is billed.

`spotTrainingSteps(work_units, checkpoint_every, interruptions)`:

- The job is finished when its progress reaches `work_units`. Each billed step adds 1 to progress.
- If `checkpoint_every` is greater than 0, the job saves a checkpoint whenever its progress is
  `checkpoint_every` units beyond the last saved point. If it is 0, nothing is ever saved.
- `interruptions` is a list of distinct billed-step numbers (counting from 1). An interruption
  happens at the **end** of that step: progress falls back to the last saved point (0 if none).
  The job then continues with the next step.
- Within one step the order is: add progress; if the job is now finished, stop; save a checkpoint
  if one is due; then apply an interruption if there is one.

Return the total number of billed steps.

**Example:** `spotTrainingSteps(8, 0, [5])` → `13` (five steps lost, then eight more)

**Example:** `spotTrainingSteps(8, 2, [5])` → `9` (only the step since the checkpoint at 4 is lost)

guide.prereqs: The SageMaker lesson (managed Spot training and checkpoints). A simple loop with state.
guide.intuition: Keep three counters: progress, the last saved progress, and billed steps. An interruption does not cost a fixed amount; it costs whatever was done since the last save, which is why frequent checkpoints matter.
hints: Put the interruption steps in a set for constant-time lookup.
Follow the stated order inside a step exactly: progress, finished?, checkpoint, interruption.
After an interruption the distance to the next checkpoint is measured from the saved point, which is where progress now stands.
guide.brute_force: The step-by-step simulation is already the direct method and is fast enough: the loop runs once per billed step.
guide.approach: Dry run `spotTrainingSteps(10, 3, [2, 5, 9])`: step 1 p=1; step 2 p=2, interrupted, back to 0; steps 3-5 p=3, checkpoint at 3, the interruption at step 5 loses nothing; steps 6-8 p=6, checkpoint; step 9 p=7, interrupted, back to 6; steps 10-12 p=9, checkpoint; step 13 p=10, finished. Answer 13.
guide.complexity: O(B) time where B is the number of billed steps, O(k) space for k interruptions.
guide.pitfalls: Resetting to zero although a checkpoint exists; applying the interruption before the checkpoint due in the same step; charging an interruption that falls on the finishing step; assuming each interruption costs exactly one step.
guide.follow_up: Without checkpoints a job longer than the typical gap between interruptions may never finish. Estimate the expected loss per interruption as half the checkpoint interval to choose that interval.

aws-health-check-state.title: Health-Check State Machine
aws-health-check-state.description:
A load balancer probes each target at a fixed interval. One failed probe does not remove a target and
one good probe does not bring it back: the state flips only after a run of **consecutive** results.

`healthStates(results, healthy_threshold, unhealthy_threshold, initial)`:

- `results`: list of booleans, one per probe (`True` = the probe succeeded).
- The target starts in state `initial` (`"healthy"` or `"unhealthy"`).
- An `unhealthy` target becomes `healthy` when the last `healthy_threshold` probes all succeeded.
- A `healthy` target becomes `unhealthy` when the last `unhealthy_threshold` probes all failed.
- Runs are counted across state changes only in the natural way: a counter of consecutive successes
  and a counter of consecutive failures, each reset to 0 by the opposite result.

Return the list of states after each probe.

**Example:** `results=[True, True, False, False, True]`, thresholds 2 and 2, initial `"unhealthy"`
→ `["unhealthy","healthy","healthy","unhealthy","unhealthy"]`
aws-health-check-state.starter:
def healthStates(results, healthy_threshold, unhealthy_threshold, initial):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The load balancing lesson: health checks and thresholds.
guide.intuition: Two counters of consecutive results. A success resets the failure counter and the other way round; a threshold reached in the 'wrong' state changes nothing.
hints: Keep `ok` and `bad`; exactly one of them is non-zero after each probe.
Check the threshold only for the transition that makes sense from the current state.
Append the state after processing each probe.
guide.brute_force: For each index look back over the last k results with a slice: O(n × k). The counters make it O(n).
guide.approach: Dry run thresholds 2/2 from unhealthy with `T T F F T`: T → ok 1 (unhealthy); T → ok 2 → healthy; F → bad 1 (healthy); F → bad 2 → unhealthy; T → ok 1 (unhealthy).
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Not resetting the opposite counter (flapping results would then accumulate); mapping each probe directly to a state; starting from the wrong initial state.

aws-alb-routing.title: Load Balancer Routing Algorithms
aws-alb-routing.description:
Simulate two ways a load balancer can choose a target.

`routeRequests(algorithm, targets, events)` returns the list of target names chosen for the `"req"`
events, in order.

- `targets`: list of `[name, weight]` in registration order (weights are non-negative integers).
- `events`: list of `["req", id]` (a new request arrives) or `["done", id]` (that request finished).

**`"weighted"`** — smooth weighted round robin. Targets with weight 0 receive nothing. Each target has
a `current` value starting at 0. For every request: add each target's weight to its `current`; pick
the target with the largest `current` (ties → earliest registered); subtract the **sum of all
weights** from the picked target's `current`. `"done"` events are ignored. Over any window of
`sum(weights)` requests each target receives exactly its weight, without long bursts.

**`"least_outstanding"`** — send each request to the target with the fewest requests in flight (ties →
earliest registered). Weights are ignored (even 0). A `"done"` event decrements the in-flight count of
the target that received that request; a `"done"` for an unknown or already finished id is ignored.

If there is no eligible target, a request yields the string `"503"`.

**Example:** `"weighted"`, targets `[["blue",3],["green",1]]`, four requests
→ `["blue","blue","green","blue"]`

guide.prereqs: The load balancing lesson: routing algorithms and weighted target groups.
guide.intuition: Weighted: every target earns credit equal to its weight on each request, and the winner pays back the total — so heavy targets win more often but never many times in a row. Least outstanding: a counter per target, incremented on assignment and decremented on completion.
hints: Filter out weight-0 targets for the weighted algorithm before anything else.
For ties use the key `(current, -index)` with `max`, or `(inflight, index)` with `min`.
Remember which target owns each request id so that `done` can find it; delete the entry so a duplicate `done` does nothing.
guide.brute_force: Expanding weights into a repeated list (`a,a,a,b`) and cycling gives the right proportions but in bursts, which is not the specified order.
guide.approach: Dry run weighted blue 3, green 1 (total 4): request 1 → current (3,1) → blue → (-1,1). Request 2 → (2,2) → tie → blue (earlier) → (-2,2). Request 3 → (1,3) → green → (1,-1). Request 4 → (4,0) → blue → (0,0). Output blue, blue, green, blue.
guide.complexity: O(E × T) for E events and T targets; O(T + in-flight requests) space.
guide.pitfalls: Bursty expansion instead of smooth round robin; decrementing twice for a duplicate `done`; applying weights to least-outstanding; crashing on an empty target list.

aws-asg-target-tracking.title: Target-Tracking Scaling Simulation
aws-asg-target-tracking.description:
A **target-tracking** policy keeps a metric near a target value by resizing the group, like a
thermostat. Simulate a simplified version minute by minute.

`targetTracking(loads, target, min_size, max_size, start, cooldown)`:

- `loads[t]`: total CPU demand during minute `t`, in "percent-instances" (150 means one and a half
  fully busy instances). With `capacity` instances the average utilisation is `loads[t] / capacity` %.
- `target`: the desired average utilisation in percent (integer ≥ 1).
- The capacity during minute 0 is `start`.
- At the end of each minute compute `desired = ceil(loads[t] / target)`, clamped to
  `[min_size, max_size]`.
  - If `desired > capacity`: **scale out immediately** — the capacity for minute `t + 1` is `desired`.
  - If `desired < capacity`: **scale in** to `desired` only if at least `cooldown` minutes have passed
    since the last capacity change of either kind (a change decided at the end of minute `c` allows a
    scale-in at the end of minute `t` when `t - c >= cooldown`). Before any change has happened,
    scale-in is allowed. Otherwise keep the capacity.
- Return the list of capacities in effect during each minute (same length as `loads`).

**Example:** `loads=[100, 300, 300, 50, 50, 50]`, target 50, min 1, max 10, start 2, cooldown 2
→ `[2, 2, 6, 6, 1, 1]`
aws-asg-target-tracking.starter:
def targetTracking(loads, target, min_size, max_size, start, cooldown):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The auto scaling lesson: target tracking, cooldowns, why scale-in is conservative.
guide.intuition: The right number of instances is 'total work divided by how much work each should carry'. Growing is urgent and unconditional; shrinking waits for a quiet period so that the group does not oscillate.
hints: Record the capacity for the minute **before** deciding the change for the next minute.
Ceiling division with integers: `-(-load // target)`.
Keep `last_change` (minute index) and update it on scale-out as well as scale-in.
guide.brute_force: Simulation is inherently linear; there is no slower sensible alternative.
guide.approach: Dry run of the example (target 50, cooldown 2, start 2). Minute 0: capacity 2, load 100 → desired 2, no change. Minute 1: capacity 2, load 300 → desired 6 > 2 → scale out, last change = 1. Minute 2: capacity 6, desired 6. Minute 3: capacity 6, load 50 → desired 1 < 6 and 3 − 1 = 2 ≥ cooldown → scale in, last change = 3. Minutes 4 and 5 run with capacity 1. Output `[2, 2, 6, 6, 1, 1]`. With cooldown 3 the scale-in would wait until the end of minute 4.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Floor instead of ceiling division; applying the cooldown to scale-out; appending the capacity after the decision (off by one minute); forgetting to clamp.

aws-asg-step-scaling.title: Step Scaling with Cooldown
aws-asg-step-scaling.description:
A **step scaling** policy reacts to an alarm with an adjustment that depends on how far the metric is
past the threshold. Simulate it.

`stepScaling(metrics, cfg)` — `metrics[t]` is the metric value (integer) observed during minute `t`;
`cfg` is a dict:

- `start`, `min`, `max`: initial capacity and bounds.
- `high`, `low`: alarm thresholds. `breach`: number of consecutive minutes required.
- `steps_out`: list of `[lower, upper, adjustment]` with `upper = null` for "no upper bound".
  `steps_in`: the same shape with negative adjustments.
- `cooldown`: minutes.

Rules, applied at the end of every minute `t` (the capacity used during minute 0 is `start`):

1. The **scale-out alarm** is in ALARM when `metrics[t] >= high` for the last `breach` consecutive
   minutes including `t`. The **scale-in alarm** is in ALARM when `metrics[t] <= low` for the last
   `breach` consecutive minutes including `t`. (`high > low`, so they are never both in ALARM.)
2. If an alarm is in ALARM and the policy is **not cooling down**, take one action:
   - scale-out: `d = metrics[t] - high`; scale-in: `d = low - metrics[t]`;
   - find the step with `lower <= d < upper` and add its adjustment to the capacity (if no step
     contains `d`, do nothing and do not start a cooldown);
   - clamp the capacity to `[min, max]`.
   An action taken at the end of minute `t` starts a cooldown: no further action can be taken at the
   end of minutes `t+1 … t+cooldown-1`; the next possible action is at the end of minute
   `t + cooldown`. An action counts (and starts the cooldown) even if clamping left the capacity
   unchanged.
3. While the alarm stays in ALARM after the cooldown, the policy acts again.

Return the capacity in effect during each minute.

**Example:** `metrics=[50, 80, 80, 80, 80, 80]`, `high=70, low=30, breach=2, cooldown=3, start=2,
min=2, max=10`, `steps_out=[[0,15,1],[15,null,3]]` → alarm at t=2 (d=10 → +1), cooldown blocks t=3
and t=4, acts again at t=5 → `[2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]`

guide.prereqs: The auto scaling lesson (step policies, alarms, cooldown) and the CloudWatch alarm problem.
guide.intuition: Three small state machines run side by side: a run counter for each alarm, and a `next_ok` minute for the cooldown. The alarm counters keep counting during the cooldown — only the action is suppressed.
hints: Append the capacity at the top of the loop, decide at the bottom.
Update both run counters on every minute, **before** checking the cooldown.
Set `next_ok = t + cooldown` only when a step actually matched.
guide.brute_force: Recomputing 'the last `breach` minutes all breach' with a slice each minute is O(n × breach); counters make it O(n).
guide.approach: Dry run of the second test: metrics `50, 90×6`, breach 2, cooldown 3. t=1 run 1. t=2 run 2 → ALARM, d = 20 → step `[15, ∞)` → +3 → capacity 5, next_ok = 5. t=3, t=4 blocked. t=5: still in alarm → +3 → 8. Output `[2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5, 8]`.
guide.complexity: O(n × S) time for S steps, O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Freezing the alarm counters during cooldown; treating `upper` as inclusive; starting a cooldown when no step matched; forgetting to clamp; letting cooldown 0 block the same minute.

aws-cloudwatch-alarm.title: CloudWatch Alarm State Evaluation
aws-cloudwatch-alarm.description:
A CloudWatch alarm watches one metric. It is configured with a threshold, a comparison, an evaluation
window of **N** datapoints and a number **M** ("M out of N datapoints must breach"). Datapoints can be
missing, and the alarm has a setting for how to treat them.

`alarmStates(datapoints, threshold, comparison, n, m, missing)`:

- `datapoints`: list of numbers or `null` (missing), one per period.
- `comparison`: one of `">"`, `">="`, `"<"`, `"<="` — a datapoint **breaches** when
  `value <comparison> threshold` is true.
- For every index `i`, produce the alarm state after period `i`:
  - if `i < n - 1` (the window is not full yet) → `"INSUFFICIENT_DATA"`;
  - otherwise look at the window `datapoints[i-n+1 .. i]` and apply the `missing` treatment:
    - `"breaching"`: a missing datapoint counts as breaching;
    - `"notBreaching"`: a missing datapoint counts as not breaching;
    - `"missing"`: if **every** datapoint in the window is missing → `"INSUFFICIENT_DATA"`;
      otherwise missing datapoints count as not breaching;
    - `"ignore"`: if every datapoint in the window is missing, the state **stays what it was** after
      the previous period (`"INSUFFICIENT_DATA"` if there is none); otherwise missing datapoints
      count as not breaching;
  - then the state is `"ALARM"` if at least `m` datapoints breach, else `"OK"`.

Return the list of states.

**Example:** `datapoints=[50, 85, 90, 40]`, threshold 80, `">"`, n=2, m=2, `"missing"`
→ `["INSUFFICIENT_DATA", "OK", "ALARM", "OK"]`
aws-cloudwatch-alarm.starter:
def alarmStates(datapoints, threshold, comparison, n, m, missing):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The CloudWatch lesson: periods, evaluation periods, datapoints to alarm, missing-data treatment.
guide.intuition: A sliding window of size N. Count breaches in it; what a hole in the data counts as depends on one setting. Two settings have a special case when the whole window is empty.
hints: Slice the window `datapoints[i-n+1 : i+1]` and split it into present and missing values.
Handle the 'all missing' cases for `missing` and `ignore` first, then fall through to the common M-of-N count.
For `ignore`, the previous state is simply the last element already appended to the output.
guide.brute_force: Re-slicing the window for each index is O(n × N); a running count would be O(n), but N is tiny in practice and the simple version is clearer.
guide.approach: Dry run `[90, 90, None, None, None, 10]`, threshold 80, `>`, N=2, M=1, treatment `ignore`: i=0 → INSUFFICIENT; i=1 window (90, 90) → ALARM; i=2 window (90, None) → one breach → ALARM; i=3 window (None, None) → keep ALARM; i=4 → keep ALARM; i=5 window (None, 10) → 0 breaches → OK. With treatment `missing`, i=3 and i=4 become INSUFFICIENT_DATA instead.
guide.complexity: O(len × N) time, O(N) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Requiring all N datapoints to breach instead of M; treating missing data as breaching by default; forgetting the comparison operator variants; reading `out[-1]` when the output is still empty.

aws-tag-compliance.title: Tag Compliance Audit
aws-tag-compliance.description:
Companies attach **tags** (key/value labels such as `Environment=prod`) to every AWS resource so that the
bill can be split by team and so that automation can find resources. An audit checks each resource
against a tagging standard.

Write `tagAudit(resources, required)`:

- `resources`: list of `{"id": str, "tags": {key: value}}`.
- `required`: dict mapping a required tag key to a list of allowed values. An **empty list** means
  "any non-blank value is acceptable".
- Tag keys and values are **case-sensitive** (as they are on AWS): `environment` does not satisfy `Environment`.
- For each resource collect problems:
  - `"missing:<Key>"` when the key is absent;
  - `"invalid:<Key>"` when the key is present but its value is blank (empty or only spaces), or is not
    in the non-empty allowed list.
- Return a list of `[id, problems]` for the non-compliant resources only, sorted by `id`, with each
  `problems` list sorted alphabetically. Compliant resources are left out.

**Example:** `resources=[{"id":"i-1","tags":{"Environment":"prod"}}]`,
`required={"Environment":["prod","dev"],"Owner":[]}` → `[["i-1", ["missing:Owner"]]]`

guide.prereqs: Dictionaries and sorting. Tags are introduced in the account and billing lesson.
guide.intuition: Loop over the standard, not over the resource's tags: for every required key ask two questions in order — is it there, and is its value acceptable?
hints: Handle one resource at a time and build its list of problems.
`value.strip() == ''` detects blank values; an empty allowed list means skip the membership check.
Only append resources whose problem list is non-empty, then sort the outer list by id and each inner list alphabetically.
guide.brute_force: There is no asymptotically worse sensible approach: a nested loop over resources and required keys is already the direct solution.
guide.approach: For each resource, read its tag dict. For each required key: absent → `missing:Key`; present but blank or outside a non-empty allowed list → `invalid:Key`. Dry run with tags `{environment: prod, Owner: ' '}` and standard `{Environment: [prod, dev], Owner: []}`: `Environment` is absent because of case → `missing:Environment`; `Owner` is blank → `invalid:Owner`. Sorted: `[invalid:Owner, missing:Environment]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(R × K) for R resources and K required keys, plus sorting; space O(output).
guide.pitfalls: Lower-casing keys (AWS tag keys are case-sensitive); forgetting blank values; returning compliant resources with an empty list; forgetting to sort.

aws-bill-estimator.title: Monthly Bill Estimator
aws-bill-estimator.description:
An AWS bill is a long list of **usage lines**: a usage type (for example `ec2:t3.micro-hours`) and a
quantity. The price of a usage type is either flat or **tiered** (the first N units cost one price, the
next units a lower one). Some usage types have a monthly **free allowance**.

Write `estimateBill(usage, prices, free)`:

- `usage`: list of `[item, quantity]`. The same item may appear on several lines; add the quantities.
- `prices[item]` is either a number (USD per unit) or a list of tiers `[[upto, price], ...]`, where
  `upto` is the cumulative upper bound of the tier in units and the last tier has `upto = null`
  (unbounded). Example: `[[10, 0.09], [null, 0.05]]` means the first 10 billable units cost 0.09 each
  and every unit after that costs 0.05.
- `free[item]` (optional) is subtracted first: `billable = max(0, total - free)`. Tiers apply to the
  billable quantity.
- An item with no entry in `prices` costs 0.

Return a list of numbers: the cost of each distinct item **in alphabetical order of item name**, then
the grand total as the last element. Do not round.

**Example:** `usage=[["s3:gb",60],["s3:gb",40]]`, `prices={"s3:gb":[[50,0.023],[null,0.022]]}`,
`free={"s3:gb":5}` → billable 95 → `50*0.023 + 45*0.022 = 2.14` → `[2.14, 2.14]`

guide.prereqs: Dictionaries; the idea of tiered pricing from the billing lesson.
guide.intuition: Three passes in a fixed order: add up quantities per item, subtract the free allowance, then walk the tiers charging each slice of the quantity at its own price. A common misreading is to charge the whole quantity at the price of the tier it ends in.
hints: First build `totals[item]` — the free allowance applies once per item, not once per line.
For tiers keep `prev`, the upper bound of the previous tier; the slice inside a tier is `min(billable, upto) - prev`.
Stop at the first tier whose bound is `None` or at least `billable`; append the sum of all costs at the end.
guide.brute_force: Charge unit by unit: for each billable unit find its tier and add that price. Correct but O(quantity), far too slow for millions of requests.
guide.approach: Aggregate, then for each item in sorted order compute `billable`. Flat price: multiply. Tiered: accumulate slices. Dry run: 180 GB out, 100 free, tiers `[[10, .09], [50, .085], [None, .07]]`: billable 80 → 10×0.09 + 40×0.085 + 30×0.07 = 0.9 + 3.4 + 2.1 = 6.4.
guide.complexity: O(L + I log I + I × T) for L usage lines, I items and T tiers; O(I) space.
guide.pitfalls: Applying the free allowance per line; pricing the full quantity at the last tier's price; forgetting the `max(0, …)` when usage is below the allowance; not handling the exact tier boundary (50 units with a 50-unit tier stays in tier one).

aws-iam-least-privilege-audit.title: Least-Privilege Policy Audit
aws-iam-least-privilege-audit.description:
**Least privilege** means a policy grants only what is used. A reviewer has the statements of an
identity policy and the list of actions the identity called in the last 90 days.

Write `auditPolicy(statements, used_actions)` returning a **sorted** list of finding strings.
Only statements with `"Effect": "Allow"` are audited. Each statement has `Sid`, `Action` (list) and
`Resource` (list).

For each Allow statement:

1. If `"*"` is in `Action` **and** `"*"` is in `Resource` → one finding `"ADMIN:<Sid>"` and nothing
   else for that statement.
2. Otherwise:
   - any action containing a `*` (such as `"*"`, `"s3:*"`, `"ec2:Describe*"`) → one finding
     `"WILDCARD_ACTION:<Sid>"` (once per statement);
   - `"*"` in `Resource` → `"WILDCARD_RESOURCE:<Sid>"`;
   - every action **without** a `*` that does not appear in `used_actions` (compare
     case-insensitively, because IAM action names are case-insensitive) → `"UNUSED:<Sid>:<action>"`
     using the action exactly as written in the policy.

**Example:** statement `{Sid:"S1", Effect:"Allow", Action:["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"], Resource:["*"]}`
with `used_actions=["s3:getobject"]` → `["UNUSED:S1:s3:PutObject", "WILDCARD_RESOURCE:S1"]`

guide.prereqs: The IAM identities lesson: what a statement, action and resource are.
guide.intuition: Each statement is judged alone. The worst case (everything on everything) gets a single label; otherwise three independent checks run.
hints: Skip Deny statements first.
Put lower-cased used actions in a set for O(1) lookups.
Emit `WILDCARD_ACTION` once per statement with `any(...)`, not once per wildcard action.
guide.brute_force: Checking each action against the `used_actions` list with a linear scan and `.lower()` on every comparison is O(A × U); a set removes the inner loop.
guide.approach: Dry run: `Action=[ec2:Describe*, ec2:StartInstances]`, resource a specific ARN, used `[ec2:DescribeInstances]`. Not admin. One action has `*` → `WILDCARD_ACTION:A`. Resource is specific → nothing. `ec2:StartInstances` has no `*` and is not used → `UNUSED:A:ec2:StartInstances`. Sort the findings.
guide.complexity: O(total actions + U) time, O(U) space.
guide.pitfalls: Case-sensitive comparison of action names; auditing Deny statements; reporting both wildcard findings as well as ADMIN; reporting a wildcard action as unused.

aws-iam-evaluate.title: IAM Policy Evaluation
aws-iam-evaluate.description:
Implement the decision AWS makes for every API call inside **one account** (a simplified but faithful
version of the real evaluation logic).

`evaluate(request, identity, resource, scps)` returns `"Allow"`, `"ExplicitDeny"` or `"ImplicitDeny"`.

- `request`: `{"principal": arn, "action": "s3:GetObject", "resource": arn, "context": {key: value}}`.
- `identity`: list of statements attached to the caller (user, group or role policies, already merged).
- `resource`: list of statements of the resource-based policy (for example a bucket policy). These
  statements also carry `"Principal"`: a list of patterns; the statement applies only if one pattern
  matches `request["principal"]`.
- `scps`: list of service control policies (each one a list of statements) inherited from the
  organisation. An empty list means the account is not in an organisation.

A **statement** has `Effect` (`"Allow"`/`"Deny"`), `Action` (list of patterns), `Resource` (list of
patterns) and optionally `Condition`.

**Matching.** In patterns `*` matches any run of characters (including none) and `?` matches exactly
one character. Actions are compared **case-insensitively**; resources and principals are
case-sensitive. A statement matches when some action pattern matches, some resource pattern matches,
(for resource policies) some principal pattern matches, and every condition holds.

**Conditions.** `Condition` is `{operator: {key: value}}`. Every entry must hold:

- `StringEquals`: the context has the key and its value equals `value`.
- `StringNotEquals`: the context does **not** have the key, or its value differs.
- `StringLike`: the context has the key and it matches `value` as a `*`/`?` pattern.

**Decision, in this order:**

1. If any matching statement in `identity`, `resource` or any SCP has `Effect: Deny` → `"ExplicitDeny"`.
2. If `scps` is non-empty, **every** SCP must contain a matching Allow statement, otherwise
   `"ImplicitDeny"`. (SCPs never grant anything; they only limit.)
3. If a matching Allow exists in `identity` **or** in `resource` → `"Allow"`.
4. Otherwise → `"ImplicitDeny"`.

**Example:** identity allows `s3:Get*` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports/*` and denies `s3:*` on
`arn:aws:s3:::reports/secret/*`. Request `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports/secret/a.txt`
→ `"ExplicitDeny"`.
aws-iam-evaluate.starter:
def evaluate(request, identity, resource, scps):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The policy evaluation lesson (explicit deny, default deny, SCPs as guardrails). Regular expressions or a hand-written wildcard matcher.
guide.intuition: Collect, for each policy source, the set of effects of the statements that match the request. The decision is then a fixed priority list: any Deny anywhere wins; SCPs must each say Allow; finally one Allow from the identity or the resource is enough. Order of statements never matters.
hints: Write `matches(statement, request)` first and test it alone: action (case-insensitive), resource, optional principal, conditions.
Translate a pattern to a regex: `*` → `.*`, `?` → `.`, escape everything else, and use `fullmatch`.
A missing context key makes `StringEquals` false but `StringNotEquals` true — that asymmetry is what makes 'deny unless region is X' block requests with no region.
guide.brute_force: Returning at the first matching statement in list order (allow-first) is the tempting approach and it is wrong: a later Deny must override an earlier Allow. A correct brute force scans all statements, which is already optimal.
guide.approach: Compute `ident`, `res` and one effect set per SCP. Dry run: admin identity, SCPs `[allow all]` and `[allow s3:* only]`, request `ec2:RunInstances`. No Deny anywhere. The second SCP has no matching Allow → `ImplicitDeny`, even though the identity policy is `*:*`. With `s3:ListBucket` both SCPs allow and the identity allows → `Allow`.
guide.complexity: O(S × P × L) for S statements, P patterns per statement and pattern/text length L (regex matching); O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Stopping at the first Allow; letting an SCP Allow grant access by itself; requiring only one SCP to allow instead of all; comparing actions case-sensitively or resources case-insensitively; treating a missing key as a match for `StringNotEquals` the wrong way round; forgetting `Principal` on resource statements; using `fnmatch`, which gives `[` a special meaning.
guide.follow_up: Real IAM adds permissions boundaries and session policies (each is another 'must also allow' layer) and cross-account rules, where the identity policy **and** the resource policy must both allow.

aws-s3-lifecycle-schedule.title: S3 Lifecycle Schedule
aws-s3-lifecycle-schedule.description:
An S3 **lifecycle configuration** is a list of rules. Each rule applies to the objects whose key starts
with the rule's prefix, moves them to colder storage classes when they reach given ages, and may
finally delete them.

Write `lifecycleSchedule(key, rules)` that returns the future of one object created on day 0 in class
`STANDARD`, as a list of `[day, state]` changes in chronological order.

- `rules`: list of `{"prefix": str, "transitions": [[days, storage_class], ...], "expire": days or null}`.
  A rule applies when `key.startswith(prefix)` (the empty prefix matches every key).
- Classes from warmest to coldest: `STANDARD`, `STANDARD_IA`, `GLACIER_IR`, `GLACIER`, `DEEP_ARCHIVE`.
- Merge the transitions of **all** applicable rules. Objects only ever move to a **colder** class:
  ignore a transition whose class is not colder than the class the object is in at that day. If
  several transitions fall on the same day, the coldest one wins (one change for that day).
- The object expires at the **smallest** `expire` among applicable rules. Expiration beats transition:
  transitions scheduled on or after the expiry day never happen. The last entry is then
  `[expiry_day, "EXPIRED"]`.
- If nothing applies, return `[]`.

**Example:** key `logs/app/1.gz`, rules `[{prefix:"logs/", transitions:[[30,"STANDARD_IA"],[90,"GLACIER"]], expire:365}]`
→ `[[30,"STANDARD_IA"],[90,"GLACIER"],[365,"EXPIRED"]]`

guide.prereqs: The S3 basics lesson (storage classes and lifecycle rules); sorting; dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Flatten everything into a timeline. Give each class a rank; walking the days in order, a transition is real only if it raises the rank. The earliest expiry cuts the timeline.
hints: Filter rules with `key.startswith(prefix)` — the prefix is a plain string, not a folder.
Group transitions by day keeping the coldest rank for that day.
Walk days in ascending order with a `current_rank`; stop at the first day that is `>= expiry`.
guide.brute_force: Simulate day by day from 0 to the largest day mentioned, asking each rule what applies today. Correct, but O(days × rules) instead of O(n log n).
guide.approach: Dry run: rules `''→[60 GLACIER]` and `logs/→[30 IA, 90 IA]` for key `logs/a`. Days: 30→IA(1), 60→GLACIER(3), 90→IA(1). Walk: day 30 rank 1 > 0 → emit; day 60 rank 3 > 1 → emit; day 90 rank 1 < 3 → ignored (objects do not warm up). Result `[[30, STANDARD_IA], [60, GLACIER]]`.
guide.complexity: O(T log T) for T transitions across matching rules; O(T) space.
guide.pitfalls: Using only the first matching rule; letting an object move back to a warmer class; emitting two changes on the same day; keeping a transition on the expiry day; treating the prefix `logs/` as matching the key `logs`.

aws-s3-storage-cost.title: S3 Monthly Storage Cost
aws-s3-storage-cost.description:
Compute one month of S3 **storage** charges (requests and data transfer are ignored) for a set of
objects, using the prices passed in.

`storageCost(objects, prices)`:

- `objects`: list of `[size_kb, storage_class, count]` — `count` identical objects of `size_kb`
  kilobytes each.
- `prices`: dict `storage_class -> USD per GB-month`. 1 GB = 1,048,576 KB.
- **Minimum billable size.** In `STANDARD_IA`, `ONEZONE_IA` and `GLACIER_IR`, an object smaller than
  128 KB is billed as 128 KB.
- **Archive overhead.** In `GLACIER` and `DEEP_ARCHIVE`, every object carries 40 KB of extra
  metadata: 32 KB billed at the object's own class price and 8 KB billed at the `STANDARD` price.
- Other classes (`STANDARD`, `INTELLIGENT_TIERING`, …) bill the exact size.

Return the total in USD (a float; do not round).

**Example:** `[[10, "STANDARD_IA", 1000000]]` with `STANDARD_IA = 0.0125`: each 10 KB object is billed as
128 KB → `128,000,000 KB = 122.07 GB` → about `1.5259`.

guide.prereqs: The S3 basics lesson: storage classes, minimum billable object size and archive overhead.
guide.intuition: Each class has its own way of turning an object's size into billable kilobytes. Convert first, price second.
hints: Work in KB until the last moment, then divide by 1,048,576.
For the infrequent-access family use `max(size, 128)`.
The archive overhead is two separate charges: 32 KB at the archive price and 8 KB at the STANDARD price.
guide.brute_force: Looping over every single object (`count` iterations) gives the same answer in O(total objects); multiplying by `count` makes it O(lines).
guide.approach: Dry run: five million 4 KB objects in DEEP_ARCHIVE at 0.00099 with STANDARD at 0.023. Archive part: 36 KB × 5,000,000 = 171.66 GB × 0.00099 = 0.170. Standard part: 8 KB × 5,000,000 = 38.15 GB × 0.023 = 0.877. Total 1.047 — more than **twice** what the same objects cost in STANDARD (19.07 GB × 0.023 = 0.439). Tiny objects do not belong in archive classes.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.
