guide.pitfalls: Using 1,000,000 KB per GB; adding all 40 KB at the archive price; applying the 128 KB minimum to STANDARD; forgetting to multiply by `count`.

aws-presigned-url-check.title: Presigned URL Expiry Check
aws-presigned-url-check.description:
A **presigned URL** lets someone without AWS credentials download or upload one S3 object for a limited
time. The signing time and lifetime travel in the query string:

`https://bucket.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/key?X-Amz-Date=20261121T101500Z&X-Amz-Expires=900&X-Amz-Signature=...`

Write `presignedStatus(url, now)` where `now` uses the same UTC format `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ`:

- Return `"INVALID"` if `X-Amz-Date` or `X-Amz-Expires` is missing, if the date is not exactly in the
  format above, or if `X-Amz-Expires` is not an integer between 1 and 604800 (seven days, the maximum
  for Signature Version 4).
- Return `"NOT_YET_VALID"` if `now` is earlier than the signing time.
- Return `"VALID"` if `signing_time <= now < signing_time + expires`.
- Otherwise return `"EXPIRED"`.

Parameter names are case-sensitive. Other parameters may appear in any order. You may assume `now` is
well formed and that dates are real calendar dates.

**Example:** date `20261121T101500Z`, expires `900`, now `20261121T102959Z` → `"VALID"`; one second
later → `"EXPIRED"`.

guide.prereqs: The S3 protection lesson (presigned URLs). String splitting; converting a calendar time to seconds with `calendar.timegm` or `datetime`.
guide.intuition: Turn both timestamps into seconds since 1970 so that the check becomes plain integer arithmetic on a half-open interval `[start, start + expires)`.
hints: Split on the first `?`, then on `&`, then each pair on the first `=`.
Validate before computing: missing keys, date format (a regex with six groups), integer range 1..604800.
Do not compare the digit strings as numbers — `20261231235950 + 30` is not a time.
guide.brute_force: There is no meaningful brute force; the mistake to avoid is arithmetic on concatenated digits instead of real time conversion.
guide.approach: Dry run: date `20261231T235950Z`, expires 30, now `20270101T000010Z`. Epoch difference is 20 seconds (10 s to midnight plus 10 s) and 20 < 30 → `VALID`, although the year changed. With digit arithmetic the answer would wrongly be EXPIRED.
guide.complexity: O(length of the URL) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Treating the end instant as valid (the interval is half-open); accepting `0` or more than seven days; case-insensitive parameter names; crashing on a URL without `?`.

aws-bucket-public-detector.title: Public Bucket Detector
aws-bucket-public-detector.description:
Most S3 data leaks come from a bucket policy that grants access to **everyone**. Write a detector.

`bucketExposure(statements, restrict_public_buckets)` returns one of
`"PRIVATE"`, `"PUBLIC_READ"`, `"PUBLIC_WRITE"`, `"PUBLIC_READ_WRITE"`, `"BLOCKED"`.

A statement is **public** when all of these hold:

1. `Effect` is `"Allow"`.
2. `Principal` is the string `"*"`, or a dict `{"AWS": "*"}`, or a dict `{"AWS": [...]}` whose list
   contains `"*"`.
3. It has **no restricting condition**. A condition restricts when, under any operator, it uses one
   of the keys `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc`, `aws:SourceVpce`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID`,
   `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:PrincipalAccount` — except that `aws:SourceIp` with the
   value `"0.0.0.0/0"` restricts nothing. Any other condition key (for example `aws:SecureTransport`)
   does not make the statement private. Condition values are strings.

A public statement gives **read** if any of its `Action` patterns matches `s3:GetObject` or
`s3:ListBucket`, and **write** if any matches `s3:PutObject` or `s3:DeleteObject`. Patterns use `*` as
a wildcard for any run of characters and are case-insensitive (`"*"`, `"s3:*"`, `"s3:Get*"`, …).
`Action` may be a string or a list.

Combine all public statements: none (or none giving read or write) → `"PRIVATE"`. Otherwise, if
`restrict_public_buckets` is `True` (the Block Public Access setting that ignores public policies) →
`"BLOCKED"`. Otherwise report read, write or both.

**Example:** `[{Effect:"Allow", Principal:"*", Action:"s3:GetObject", Resource:"arn:aws:s3:::site/*"}]`,
`False` → `"PUBLIC_READ"`.

guide.prereqs: The S3 protection lesson: bucket policies, the `Principal` element, Block Public Access.
guide.intuition: Three filters decide whether a statement is public (effect, principal, absence of a real restriction); then two probes decide what it exposes. Block Public Access is applied last, and only when something was actually exposed.
hints: Write `is_public_principal` for the three accepted shapes.
A condition restricts only if its key is in the given set, with the `0.0.0.0/0` exception.
Test each action pattern against four probe actions with a wildcard matcher; do not try to enumerate prefixes.
guide.brute_force: String-prefix tests such as `startswith('s3:get')` look simpler but miss patterns like `s3:*Object` and wrongly flag `s3:GetBucketLocation`.
guide.approach: Dry run: statements `[List* with PrincipalOrgID condition, DeleteObject without condition]`. First statement: public principal but restricted → skipped. Second: public, no condition, matches `s3:DeleteObject` → write. Result `PUBLIC_WRITE`.
guide.complexity: O(S × A) pattern matches; O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: Returning BLOCKED for a bucket that had nothing public; treating any condition as a restriction (`aws:SecureTransport` only forces HTTPS); forgetting the dict forms of `Principal`; flagging Deny statements; case-sensitive action matching.

aws-lambda-cost.title: Lambda Monthly Cost
aws-lambda-cost.description:
Lambda bills two things: the **number of requests** and the **compute time**, measured in
*GB-seconds* (memory configured in GB × seconds of execution).

`lambdaCost(invocations, avg_ms, memory_mb, pricing)`:

- `invocations`: number of invocations in the month; `avg_ms`: average billed duration in
  milliseconds (integer); `memory_mb`: configured memory.
- `gb_seconds = invocations × (avg_ms / 1000) × (memory_mb / 1024)`.
- `pricing` has `per_million_requests`, `per_gb_second`, `free_requests` and `free_gb_seconds`.
  The free amounts are subtracted first and can never make a part negative.
- `cost = max(0, invocations − free_requests) / 1,000,000 × per_million_requests
          + max(0, gb_seconds − free_gb_seconds) × per_gb_second`.

Return the cost in USD (float, not rounded).

**Example:** 5,000,000 invocations of 200 ms at 512 MB with `0.20` per million, `0.0000166667` per
GB-second, 1,000,000 free requests and 400,000 free GB-seconds → GB-seconds = 500,000 →
`4 × 0.20 + 100000 × 0.0000166667 = 2.4667`.
aws-lambda-cost.starter:
def lambdaCost(invocations, avg_ms, memory_mb, pricing):
    pass
aws-lambda-cost.solution:
def lambdaCost(invocations, avg_ms, memory_mb, pricing):
    gb_seconds = invocations * (avg_ms / 1000) * (memory_mb / 1024)
    req = max(0, invocations - pricing["free_requests"]) / 1e6 * pricing["per_million_requests"]
    compute = max(0, gb_seconds - pricing["free_gb_seconds"]) * pricing["per_gb_second"]
    return req + compute

guide.prereqs: The Lambda lesson: the pricing model (requests plus GB-seconds).
guide.intuition: Two meters, each with its own free allowance. Compute each meter, subtract the allowance with a floor at zero, multiply by its price, add.
hints: Convert milliseconds to seconds and megabytes to gigabytes (÷ 1024) before multiplying.
Use `max(0, …)` on each part separately — unused free requests do not offset compute.
The request price is per million.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable.
guide.approach: Dry run: 1,000,000 invocations × 3.2 s × 0.125 GB = 400,000 GB-seconds — exactly the free allowance, and exactly the free request count → cost 0. One more invocation costs 0.0000002 for the request plus 0.4 GB-seconds of compute.
guide.pitfalls: Negative parts when usage is below the free tier; dividing memory by 1000; forgetting that doubling memory doubles the GB-seconds for the same duration.

aws-lambda-concurrency.title: Lambda Concurrency and Cold Starts
aws-lambda-concurrency.description:
Lambda runs each concurrent request in its own **execution environment**. A new environment needs a
**cold start**; a finished environment stays warm for a while and can serve the next request without
one. An account-level **concurrency limit** caps the number of busy environments.

`lambdaStats(invocations, idle_timeout, limit)`:

- `invocations`: list of `[start_ms, duration_ms]`, sorted by `start_ms` (ties keep list order).
  An invocation that runs occupies its environment during `[start, start + duration)`.
- For each invocation, in order:
  1. A **warm** environment is one that is free (`free_at <= start`) and has not been idle for more
     than `idle_timeout` (`start - free_at <= idle_timeout`). Environments idle for longer are gone.
     If warm environments exist, reuse the one that became free **most recently** (largest
     `free_at`).
  2. Otherwise, if the number of busy environments (`free_at > start`) is below `limit`, create a new
     environment: one cold start.
  3. Otherwise the invocation is **throttled**: it does not run at all.
- Return `[cold_starts, peak_concurrency, throttled]`, where peak concurrency is the largest number
  of invocations running at the same instant.

**Example:** `[[0,100],[50,100],[120,10],[5000,10]]`, idle timeout 1000, limit 10 → the first two
overlap (2 cold starts, peak 2), the third reuses a warm environment, the fourth arrives after every
environment has expired (cold) → `[3, 2, 0]`.
aws-lambda-concurrency.solution:
def lambdaStats(invocations, idle_timeout, limit):
    envs = []            # free_at time of each live environment
    cold = peak = throttled = 0
    for start, dur in invocations:
        envs = [f for f in envs if f > start or start - f <= idle_timeout]
        warm = [f for f in envs if f <= start]
        busy = len(envs) - len(warm)
        if warm:
            envs.remove(max(warm))
        elif busy < limit:
            cold += 1
        else:
            throttled += 1
            continue
        envs.append(start + dur)
        peak = max(peak, sum(1 for f in envs if f > start))
    return [cold, peak, throttled]

guide.prereqs: The Lambda lesson: execution environments, cold starts, concurrency limits and throttling.
guide.intuition: Keep one number per live environment: the time it becomes free. Each arrival first forgets expired environments, then prefers a warm one, then a new one if the limit allows.
hints: An environment is busy at `start` when `free_at > start`, warm when `free_at <= start` and `start - free_at <= idle_timeout`.
Drop expired environments before counting anything.
Peak concurrency can be measured right after each successful start: count the environments with `free_at > start`.
guide.brute_force: Checking every millisecond of the timeline for the number of running invocations works but is O(time range). Event-based accounting is O(n × environments).
guide.approach: Dry run with limit 2 and four 1000 ms invocations at 0, 1, 2, 3: first → cold (busy 0 < 2); second → cold (busy 1 < 2); third → no warm, busy 2 = limit → throttled; fourth → throttled. Result `[2, 2, 2]`.
guide.complexity: O(n × e) time for n invocations and e live environments (a heap would give O(n log e)); O(e) space.
guide.pitfalls: Reusing an environment that is still busy; using `<` instead of `<=` at the exact boundary (an environment that frees at t can serve a request at t, and one idle for exactly `idle_timeout` is still warm); counting throttled invocations as running; reusing the oldest warm environment instead of the most recently freed.

aws-dynamodb-capacity.title: DynamoDB Capacity Units
aws-dynamodb-capacity.description:
In provisioned mode you tell DynamoDB how many **read capacity units** (RCU) and **write capacity
units** (WCU) a table needs.

- One RCU = one **strongly consistent** read per second of an item up to **4 KB**. Larger items need
  one unit per started 4 KB. An **eventually consistent** read costs half; a **transactional** read
  costs double.
- One WCU = one write per second of an item up to **1 KB**; one unit per started 1 KB. A
  **transactional** write costs double.

`capacityUnits(item_bytes, reads_per_s, writes_per_s, mode)` with `mode` in `"eventual"`, `"strong"`,
`"transactional"` (the mode applies to reads; writes are doubled only in transactional mode).
1 KB = 1024 bytes. An item of 0 bytes still counts as one unit per operation.

Return `[rcu, wcu]` as integers; when the eventual-consistency halving gives a fraction, round the
**total** up.

**Example:** 6,000-byte items, 100 reads/s, 20 writes/s, `"eventual"` → each read needs 2 units,
halved → 100 RCU; each write needs 6 units → 120 WCU → `[100, 120]`.
aws-dynamodb-capacity.starter:
def capacityUnits(item_bytes, reads_per_s, writes_per_s, mode):
    pass
aws-dynamodb-capacity.solution:
def capacityUnits(item_bytes, reads_per_s, writes_per_s, mode):
    read_units = max(1, -(-item_bytes // 4096))
    write_units = max(1, -(-item_bytes // 1024))
    rcu = reads_per_s * read_units
    wcu = writes_per_s * write_units
    if mode == "eventual":
        rcu = -(-rcu // 2)
    elif mode == "transactional":
        rcu *= 2
        wcu *= 2
    return [rcu, wcu]

guide.prereqs: The DynamoDB lesson: capacity modes, RCU and WCU.
guide.intuition: Round **each item** up to its block size first (4 KB for reads, 1 KB for writes), multiply by the rate, then apply the mode's factor to the total.
hints: `-(-n // block)` is integer ceiling division; force a minimum of 1.
Halve the total RCU for eventual reads and round that total up.
Transactional doubles both reads and writes.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable.
guide.approach: Dry run: 1,025-byte items, 7 reads and 7 writes per second, eventual. Read block: 1 unit each → 7 → halved 3.5 → 4 RCU. Write: 1,025 bytes spans 2 KB → 14 WCU. Result `[4, 14]`.
guide.pitfalls: Multiplying the rate by the fractional size before rounding (10 reads of 4,097 bytes is 20 units, not 11); halving per item instead of in total; forgetting writes use 1 KB blocks.

aws-gsi-projection.title: GSI Projection Check
aws-gsi-projection.description:
A **global secondary index** (GSI) is a copy of part of a table, organised under a different key. The
copy contains only the attributes that were **projected** into it — and a query on a GSI can never
fetch the rest from the base table.

`missingAttributes(table_keys, index, requested)`:

- `table_keys`: list with the table's partition key and, optionally, sort key attribute names.
- `index`: `{"keys": [index partition key, optional index sort key], "projection": "KEYS_ONLY" |
  "INCLUDE" | "ALL", "include": [names]}` (`include` is only meaningful for `"INCLUDE"`).
- `requested`: attribute names the query wants back.

Attributes available in the index: the index keys and the table keys (always), plus the `include`
list for `INCLUDE`, or everything for `ALL`.

Return the sorted list of requested attributes that the index **cannot** return (duplicates removed).
An empty list means the index covers the query.

**Example:** table keys `["order_id"]`, index keys `["customer_id","created_at"]`, `KEYS_ONLY`,
requested `["order_id","total","status"]` → `["status","total"]`

guide.prereqs: The DynamoDB lesson: global secondary indexes and projections. Python sets.
guide.intuition: Build the set of attributes that physically live in the index, subtract it from the requested set.
hints: `ALL` short-circuits to an empty answer.
Table keys are always projected, even with `KEYS_ONLY`.
Only honour `include` when the projection type is `INCLUDE`.
guide.brute_force: A nested loop comparing each requested name with each available name is O(r × a); sets make it O(r + a).
guide.approach: Dry run: table keys `[pk, sk]`, index keys `[gsi1pk]`, KEYS_ONLY with a stray include list `[ignored]`. Available = {pk, sk, gsi1pk}. Requesting `[ignored]` → missing `[ignored]`, because the include list does not apply to KEYS_ONLY.
guide.complexity: O(r + a) time and space, plus O(m log m) to sort the m missing names.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting that table keys are always in the index; honouring `include` for `KEYS_ONLY`; returning duplicates or unsorted output; case-insensitive comparison (attribute names are case-sensitive).

aws-dynamodb-hot-partition.title: Hot Partition Key Detector
aws-dynamodb-hot-partition.description:
DynamoDB spreads items over partitions by hashing the **partition key**. If a few key values receive
most of the traffic, their partitions are throttled while the rest of the table sits idle — a **hot
partition**. Given a sample of requests, find the hot keys and suggest whether write sharding helps.

`hotKeys(accesses, threshold_pct, shards)`:

- `accesses`: list of partition-key values (strings), one per sampled request.
- A key is **hot** when its share of all requests is **strictly greater** than `threshold_pct`
  percent (use integer arithmetic: `count × 100 > threshold_pct × total`).
- Write sharding appends a suffix `#0 … #(shards-1)` to a key, splitting its traffic evenly over
  `shards` new keys. For each hot key compute `after = ceil(count / shards)`, the traffic of its
  busiest shard; sharding **fixes** the key when `after × 100 <= threshold_pct × total`.

Return a list of `[key, count, fixed]` for the hot keys, sorted by `count` descending and then by key
ascending; `fixed` is a boolean. Return `[]` when `accesses` is empty.

**Example:** `["a","a","a","b","c","a","d","a"]`, threshold 25, shards 2 → `a` has 5 of 8 (62.5 %);
after sharding its busiest shard gets 3 of 8 (37.5 %) → `[["a", 5, False]]`.

guide.prereqs: The DynamoDB lesson: partition keys, hot partitions and write sharding. Counting with a dictionary.
guide.intuition: Count, compare each share with the threshold without floating point, then ask whether dividing the count by the shard number brings the busiest piece under the same threshold.
hints: Cross-multiply instead of dividing: `count × 100 > threshold × total`.
The busiest shard after an even split has `ceil(count / shards)` requests.
Sort with the key `(-count, key)`.
guide.brute_force: Calling `accesses.count(k)` for every distinct key is O(n × distinct); a dictionary pass is O(n).
guide.approach: Dry run: 900 requests for tenant-1 and 100 other tenants once each (total 1000), threshold 10 %, 10 shards. tenant-1: 90 % > 10 % → hot. After sharding: ceil(900 / 10) = 90 → 9 % ≤ 10 % → fixed. With 9 shards: 100 → 10 % ≤ 10 % → still fixed (the fix test is not strict).
guide.complexity: O(n + h log h) time for n accesses and h hot keys; O(distinct keys) space.
guide.pitfalls: Using `>=` for the hot test; floor instead of ceiling for the shard split; floating-point percentages at the boundary; sorting by key only.

aws-dynamodb-query-scan.title: Query vs Scan Read Cost
aws-dynamodb-query-scan.description:
A DynamoDB **Query** reads only the items of one partition key (optionally a range of sort keys). A
**Scan** reads the whole table. In both cases a **filter** is applied *after* the items are read, so
it reduces what is returned but not what is paid for.

`readCost(items, request)`:

- `items`: list of dicts with `"pk"`, `"sk"` (strings), `"size"` (bytes) and other attributes.
- `request`: `{"op": "query"|"scan", "pk": str or null, "sk_lo": str or null, "sk_hi": str or null,
  "filter": [attribute, value] or null, "consistent": bool}`.
- Items **read**:
  - `scan`: every item;
  - `query`: items with `pk == request["pk"]`, and if `sk_lo`/`sk_hi` are given, with
    `sk_lo <= sk <= sk_hi` (string comparison; either bound may be `null` = open).
- Items **returned**: the items read that also satisfy the filter (`item.get(attribute) == value`),
  or all the items read if there is no filter.
- **Consumed read capacity**: add the sizes of all items read, divide by 4096 and round up (the
  rounding is on the total of the operation, not per item); 0 items read → 0. If `consistent` is
  `False`, halve the result (this can give `x.5`).

Return `[consumed_rcu, returned_count]`.

**Example:** a table of 14 items; `query` on `pk="user#1"` reads 10 items of 1,500 bytes → 15,000
bytes → 4 RCU strongly consistent, 2.0 eventually consistent.

guide.prereqs: The DynamoDB lesson: Query, Scan, filter expressions and read capacity.
guide.intuition: Separate two sets: what the operation touches (decided by the key condition only) and what it returns (after the filter). Capacity is charged on the first set.
hints: Build `read` from the key condition alone; never look at the filter in that step.
Sum the sizes of `read`, then one ceiling division by 4096.
For eventually consistent reads divide by two with `/` — a half unit is a valid answer.
guide.brute_force: Both operations are linear passes here. The lesson of the problem is that, in the real service, a Scan is linear in the size of the **table**, while a Query is linear in the size of the **partition**.
guide.approach: Dry run: scan with filter `pk = user#3` over the sample table: reads 10 × 1,500 + 3 × 5,000 + 300 = 30,300 bytes → ceil(30,300 / 4096) = 8 RCU and returns 1 item. The equivalent query on `pk = user#3` reads 300 bytes → 1 RCU for the same single item.
guide.complexity: O(n) time over the items; O(n) space for the lists (O(1) with counters).
guide.pitfalls: Applying the filter before computing the cost; rounding each item up separately (that is the GetItem rule, not the Query/Scan rule); integer-dividing the eventually consistent result; treating `None` bounds as strings.

aws-rds-failover-lag.title: Multi-AZ Failover vs Read-Replica Promotion
aws-rds-failover-lag.description:
A primary database fails at time `failure`. What it costs depends on how it was protected:

- **`"multi-az"`** — a standby in another Availability Zone is updated **synchronously**: every
  committed write is on the standby. Recovery is an automatic failover.
- **`"read-replica"`** — a replica is updated **asynchronously** and lags behind by `lag` seconds:
  writes committed during the last `lag` seconds before the failure never reached it. Recovery is a
  promotion of the replica.
- **`"backup"`** — only automated backups: the database can be restored to the latest restorable
  time, which is `backup_interval` seconds granular. Writes after the last backup point are lost.

`recoveryOutcome(setup, failure, writes, cfg)`:

- `writes`: list of commit times (integers, any order). Writes with a time `> failure` were rejected
  by the application and are ignored. Writes at or before `failure` were committed on the primary.
- `cfg` has `failover_s`, `promote_s`, `restore_s`, `lag`, `backup_interval`.
- Lost writes:
  - `multi-az`: none;
  - `read-replica`: committed writes with `time > failure - lag`;
  - `backup`: backup points are at `0, backup_interval, 2 × backup_interval, …`; the last one at or
    before `failure` is `last = (failure // backup_interval) × backup_interval`; committed writes with
    `time > last` are lost.
- Downtime: `failover_s`, `promote_s` or `restore_s` respectively.

Return `[downtime_seconds, lost_writes, achieved_rpo_seconds]`, where the achieved RPO is how far back
in time the data went: `0` for multi-az, `lag` for read-replica, `failure - last` for backup.

**Example:** failure at 1000, writes `[100, 990, 996, 1000, 1003]`, lag 5 → read-replica loses the
writes at 996 and 1000 → `[promote_s, 2, 5]`.
aws-rds-failover-lag.starter:
def recoveryOutcome(setup, failure, writes, cfg):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The RDS and Aurora lesson: Multi-AZ (synchronous standby), read replicas (asynchronous), automated backups; RTO and RPO from the reliability lesson.
guide.intuition: Each protection scheme defines a cut-off time: everything committed after it is gone. Synchronous replication puts the cut-off at the failure itself; asynchronous replication puts it `lag` seconds earlier; backups put it at the last backup point.
hints: Discard writes after the failure first — they were never committed.
Count the committed writes strictly later than the cut-off.
Integer division gives the last backup point: `(failure // interval) × interval`.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable; one pass over the writes.
guide.approach: Dry run of the third test (backup every 300 s, failure at 1000): last backup point = 900. Committed writes `[100, 990, 996, 1000]`; later than 900: three → lost 3; achieved RPO = 100 s; downtime = restore time 3600 s. Multi-AZ on the same data: downtime 90 s, nothing lost.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Counting rejected writes (after the failure) as lost; off-by-one at the cut-off (a write exactly at the cut-off time is safe); confusing a read replica with a standby — a replica is for read scaling and loses recent writes when promoted.

aws-dr-strategy.title: Disaster-Recovery Strategy Selector
aws-dr-strategy.description:
The four classic disaster-recovery strategies trade money for speed: **backup and restore**, **pilot
light**, **warm standby** and **multi-site active/active**. Each offers a recovery time objective
(**RTO**: how long the service may be down) and a recovery point objective (**RPO**: how much recent
data may be lost), at a monthly cost.

`chooseStrategy(rto_min, rpo_min, budget, strategies)`:

- `strategies`: list of `[name, rto_minutes, rpo_minutes, monthly_cost]`.
- A strategy **qualifies** when its RTO ≤ `rto_min` and its RPO ≤ `rpo_min`.
- Among the qualifying strategies that also cost ≤ `budget`, return the name of the cheapest. Break
  ties by lower RTO, then lower RPO, then name.
- If some strategies qualify but all of them are over budget, return
  `"OVER_BUDGET:<name>"` with the cheapest qualifying one (same tie-breaks) — the business must either
  pay or relax the objectives.
- If nothing qualifies, return `"IMPOSSIBLE"`.

**Example:** strategies backup-restore (1440, 1440, 100), pilot-light (60, 15, 600), warm-standby
(10, 1, 2500), multi-site (0, 0, 9000). Requirement RTO 30 min, RPO 5 min, budget 3000 →
`"warm-standby"`. With budget 1000 → `"OVER_BUDGET:warm-standby"`.
aws-dr-strategy.starter:
def chooseStrategy(rto_min, rpo_min, budget, strategies):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The reliability lesson: RTO, RPO and the four disaster-recovery strategies.
guide.intuition: Objectives are hard constraints, cost is what you minimise. Filter on the objectives first; the budget only decides between a clean answer and an 'over budget' warning.
hints: Build tuples `(cost, rto, rpo, name)` so that `min` applies every tie-break at once.
Distinguish three cases: nothing qualifies, something qualifies within budget, something qualifies but only above budget.
The over-budget answer uses the cheapest qualifying strategy, not the fastest.
guide.brute_force: Sorting all strategies is O(n log n); a single `min` is O(n). Either is fine for four strategies.
guide.approach: Dry run: RTO ≤ 30, RPO ≤ 5. backup-restore fails both; pilot-light fails both (60, 15); warm-standby (10, 1) and multi-site (0, 0) qualify. Budget 3000 → warm-standby (2500). Budget 1000 → neither is affordable → `OVER_BUDGET:warm-standby`.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Choosing the most resilient option instead of the cheapest sufficient one; returning IMPOSSIBLE when the real problem is budget; wrong tie-break order.
